docs.title: Codex Praedium: Open-Source Governance & Statutory Standards for Agentic AI
docs.text:
Consumer protection requires a fiduciary in the loop. An initiative of the American Real Estate Association (ARA), the Real Estate AI Task Force builds enforceable, state-level statutory frameworks and technical standards to ensure autonomous AI systems never replace human fiduciary accountability in real estate transactions. 

Review Model Legislation Join the Task Force

docs.title: The Systemic Challenge: Autonomous Bots Without Accountability
docs.text:
Real estate is entering the era of Agentic AI—autonomous software systems capable of browsing listings, communicating with buyers and sellers, negotiating terms, and generating binding contracts in continuous loops without human intervention. 

Across multiple states, unlicensed software operators and thin-broker platforms are already deploying autonomous bots to perform regulated brokerage activities for compensation—hiding behind software Terms of Service while disclaiming all fiduciary duty, legal liability, and regulatory oversight. 

The Regulatory Vacuum

Real estate licensing lives in state capitals, not Washington, D.C. While legacy trade institutions remain paralyzed by internal bureaucracy or focused on federal preemption, state real estate commissioners lack clear statutory mandates and enforcement teeth to stop unlicensed autonomous platforms before consumer harm becomes widespread.

docs.title: Our Mandate: Licensee-in-the-Loop
docs.text:
We do not seek to ban AI innovation or restrict legitimate productivity tools used by licensed professionals. Instead, we draw a bright, enforceable legal line between software tools and fiduciary representation: 

The Fiduciary Mandate: Whenever an automated or agentic AI system performs regulated real estate brokerage activity—including drafting offers, negotiating terms, or advising consumers on property transactions—it must operate under the direct, identifiable supervision of a state-licensed human professional who reviews, signs off on, and retains full fiduciary accountability for the outcome.

docs.title: Why Open-Source Governance?
docs.text:
For decades, real estate policy has been drafted behind closed doors by insulated committees—resulting in reactive compromises, technical blind spots, and unworkable mandates. 

Codex Praedium (Code of Real Property) replaces secret committees with an Open-Core Policy Model: 

  • Radical Transparency: Every draft of our model legislation, technical checkpoint, and public comment is published openly on GitHub and reviewed in public forums.
  • Cross-Disciplinary Rigor: We unite brokerage CTOs, AI engineers, managing brokers, real estate attorneys, and frontline practitioners so statutes work both in the courtroom and in production code.
  • Strict Vendor Neutrality: Governed by an ironclad Vendor Neutrality Firewall, our standards apply equally to traditional brokerages, virtual firms, teams, and digital platforms—with zero proprietary carve-outs.

docs.title: The 3-Point Legislative Litmus Test
docs.text:
We welcome collaboration with any lawmaker, state regulator, or industry association. We evaluate all proposed state AI legislation against three objective benchmarks: 

# Benchmark Core Requirement Why It Matters 1 Identifiable Fiduciary Requires a named, state-licensed human professional to be clearly disclosed to the consumer for any automated transaction workflow. Eliminates "black-box" anonymity so consumers always know who owes them loyalty and care. 2 Pre-Execution Human Sign-Off Mandates human licensee review and approval before any offer, counteroffer, or binding contractual term is transmitted. Prevents probabilistic AI hallucinations or missed addenda from binding consumers to costly errors. 3 Direct Enforcement Teeth Empowers state real estate commissioners to investigate, fine, and enjoin unlicensed software operators—not just police existing agents. Stops regulatory deflection where agencies only audit licensed brokers while ignoring illegal tech startups.

docs.title: Statehouse Momentum & Rollout
docs.text:
Unlike traditional committees that spend years "monitoring trends," our model statutory language is actively advancing in state capitals: 

  • New York: Bicameral draft legislation under active review by State Senate and Assembly sponsors ahead of the upcoming legislative session.
  • Florida & Maryland: Model statutory language circulating with state legislators and policy advisors.
  • California & Texas: Active gap-analysis and stakeholder recruitment targeting high-volume middle markets and broker supervision reform.

docs.title: Why Open-Source Governance?
docs.text:
For decades, real estate industry policy has been drafted behind closed doors by small, insulated committees—resulting in reactive compromises, technical blind spots, and unworkable statutory mandates.

Codex Praedium (Code of Real Property) replaces secret committees with an Open-Core Policy Model. By publishing our working drafts, public comments, and legislative scorecards openly on GitHub, we ensure every rule is stress-tested by frontline practitioners, software architects, managing brokers, and legal experts before it reaches a statehouse floor.

docs.title: Three-Tier Open-Core Operating Model
docs.text:
To combine radical transparency with rigorous legislative execution, the Real Estate AI Task Force operates under a three-tier governance architecture modeled on modern open-source standards:

Tier Structure Who Participates Authority & Role Tier 1 Public RFC Portal Open to all licensed agents, brokers, engineers, consumers, and allied professionals. Submit real-world edge cases, technical critiques, and line-by-line feedback on published drafts. All substantive submissions are archived publicly. Tier 2 Stakeholder Advisory Panels Invited specialists segmented into four dedicated tracks (Technical, Brokerage Ops, State Legal, Consumer). Review public RFCs, identify statutory loopholes, and test implementation feasibility across firms of all sizes. Tier 3 Core Drafting Committee Task Force Chair, ARA Executive Leadership, and designated legal/policy counsel. Holds final editorial and commit authority over model statutory text and official white papers to ensure legal precision and constitutional soundness.

docs.title: Segmented Advisory Tracks
docs.text:
To prevent institutional inertia or business-side hesitation from silencing technical realities, Tier 2 advisory contributors are organized into four focused tracks:

  1. Technical & AI Systems Track: Brokerage CTOs, ML engineers, and PropTech architects stress-testing human-in-the-loop checkpoints, audit logs, and API boundaries.
  2. Brokerage Operations & Supervision Track: Managing brokers and compliance officers ensuring supervision rules scale cleanly across independent firms, teams, and national brokerages.
  3. State Legislative & Legal Track: Real estate attorneys, former regulators, and ARA State Policy Chairs (prioritizing NY, FL, MD, CA, and TX).
  4. Consumer & Fiduciary Advocacy Track: Consumer protection advocates and housing policy analysts evaluating buyer and seller liability risks.

docs.title: Code of Discourse
docs.text:
To ensure our work products command immediate respect from state legislators, attorneys general, and real estate commissioners, all Task Force participants must adhere to three non-negotiable rules:

1. Consumer Safety Over Protectionism: All policy arguments must center strictly on fiduciary duty, legal liability, data integrity, and consumer harm. Rhetoric aimed at restricting competition, fixing fees, or blocking legitimate productivity tools is off-mission and will be archived out of policy tracks.

2. Strict Vendor Neutrality: Task Force forums are for public policy, not product promotion. No participant—including Task Force leadership—may pitch, demo, or solicit business for commercial software products within Task Force channels or documents.

3. Separate Operations from Marketing: Discussions regarding everyday marketing tools (such as virtual staging disclosures or copywriting prompts) are routed to practitioner best-practice threads so our statutory track remains laser-focused on unlicensed autonomous practice and broker supervision.

docs.title: Vendor Neutrality & Conflict Firewall
docs.text:
Effective technology policy requires builders who understand how autonomous AI systems work—paired with licensed brokers who carry real-world fiduciary liability. To maintain absolute institutional integrity, the Task Force enforces an ironclad Vendor Neutrality Firewall:

  • Zero Commercial Infrastructure Overlap: The Task Force is an independent policy initiative of the American Real Estate Association (ARA). It does not share user data, member rosters, or communication platforms with any commercial brokerage or PropTech company (including MarketWhiffs, Inc.).
  • Model-Neutral Statutory Standards: Our Licensee-in-the-Loop framework applies equally to every business model—traditional brick-and-mortar brokerages, virtual firms, teams, and digital platforms alike. Every licensed entity must meet the exact same human-supervision and fiduciary accountability standards, with zero proprietary carve-outs.
  • Strict Non-Solicitation: Task Force repositories, working groups, and public comment portals are restricted exclusively to policy analysis. Any attempt to pitch software, recruit agents, or solicit consumer leads results in immediate removal.
  • Public Auditability: Every version of our model legislation and technical standards is maintained in a public Git repository with a transparent commit history, allowing any broker, regulator, or competing trade association to verify that the text serves the public interest.

docs.title: Model Legislation: The Fiduciary AI Accountability Act
Statutory Purpose & Legislative Intent
docs.text:
State real estate licensing laws exist to protect the public from fraud, misrepresentation, and unvetted financial risk during the largest transaction of a consumer's life. While Artificial Intelligence offers powerful productivity benefits for licensed professionals, autonomous Agentic AI systems are increasingly deployed by unlicensed software operators and minimally supervised platforms to perform regulated brokerage activities for compensation.

The Fiduciary AI Accountability Act establishes a clear, technology-neutral statutory boundary: software may assist in a transaction, but it may never replace a state-licensed human fiduciary.

docs.title: 1. Prohibition on Unlicensed Autonomous Brokerage
docs.text:
• Bright-Line Rule: No person, corporation, or software platform may deploy an autonomous or semi-autonomous AI system to perform regulated real estate brokerage activities—including property valuation advice, offer generation, contract negotiation, or buyer/seller representation—for compensation without holding an active state real estate brokerage license.
  • Terms of Service Invalidation: Software Terms of Service or end-user disclaimers cannot waive state licensing requirements, fiduciary duties, or statutory liability when a system performs regulated brokerage acts.

docs.title: 2. Mandatory Licensee-in-the-Loop Oversight
docs.text:
• Identifiable Supervising Licensee: Every consumer-facing AI workflow performing regulated activities must be explicitly tethered to a named, state-licensed human practitioner whose license number and supervising brokerage are clearly disclosed to the consumer at the outset of interaction.
  • Pre-Execution Human Sign-Off: Before any AI-generated offer, counteroffer, lease, addendum, or material contractual term is transmitted to a counterparty or binding system, a licensed human professional must review, verify, and execute an auditable sign-off.
  • Non-Delegable Accountability: The supervising licensee and managing broker retain 100% legal, regulatory, and fiduciary accountability for all representations and contractual terms generated by their authorized AI systems.

docs.title: 3. Modernized Broker Supervision Standards
docs.text:
• Model-Neutral Compliance: Supervision standards apply equally across all licensed entities—traditional brick-and-mortar brokerages, virtual firms, teams, and digital platforms—eliminating "thin-broker" loopholes where a single license rubber-stamps unmonitored bots.
  • Audit Trail Retention: Brokerages utilizing AI systems for transaction workflows must maintain immutable, timestamped audit logs capturing AI outputs, human review checkpoints, and final licensee approvals for standard statutory retention periods.

docs.title: 4. Direct Regulatory Enforcement Teeth
docs.text:
• Jurisdiction Over Unlicensed Operators: Explicitly empowers State Real Estate Commissioners and Attorneys General to investigate, issue cease-and-desist orders, levy civil penalties, and seek injunctive relief against unlicensed technology operators engaging in de facto brokerage.
  • Consumer Private Right of Action: Preserves consumer remedies when unlicensed autonomous platforms cause material financial harm through misrepresentation or contractual error.

docs.title: Technical Reference Implementation: Pre-Execution Gate
docs.text:
To ensure statutory definitions align with modern software engineering practices, Codex Praedium provides reference validation patterns for brokerage engineering teams. Any automated workflow that prepares binding transaction documents must enforce a deterministic human-in-the-loop gate before external transmission:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime
from typing import Optional

@dataclass
class TransactionArtifact:
    artifact_id: str
    content: str
    generated_by_ai: bool
    assigned_licensee_id: str
    supervising_broker_id: str
    reviewed_by_licensee_id: Optional[str] = None
    approved_at: Optional[datetime] = None

def can_transmit_to_consumer(artifact: TransactionArtifact) -> bool:
    """
    Enforces the Licensee-in-the-Loop pre-execution checkpoint.
    Returns True only when a named licensee has verified the artifact.
    """
    if not artifact.assigned_licensee_id or not artifact.supervising_broker_id:
        raise PermissionError("Missing identifiable fiduciary assignment.")

    if artifact.generated_by_ai:
        if not artifact.reviewed_by_licensee_id or artifact.approved_at is None:
            return False
        if artifact.reviewed_by_licensee_id != artifact.assigned_licensee_id:
            raise PermissionError("Approving licensee must match assigned fiduciary.")

    return True

docs.title: Statehouse Rollout & Priority Jurisdictions
docs.text:
Because real estate licensing is governed by state law rather than federal preemption, the Task Force focuses on tailored statehouse execution:

Maryland Policy Advisor Review Adapting model statutory definitions for state licensing commission oversight and consumer disclosure clarity. docs.title: Evaluating Rival Proposals: The 3-Point Litmus Test
docs.text:
Lawmakers, regulators, and members can benchmark any proposed state AI bill against our three non-negotiable criteria:

  1. Identifiable Fiduciary: Does the statute require a named, state-licensed human professional to be disclosed to the consumer?
  2. Pre-Execution Human Sign-Off: Does it mandate human licensee review before binding terms or offers are transmitted?
  3. Direct Enforcement Teeth: Does it empower state commissioners to fine and enjoin unlicensed software operators, rather than solely policing existing licensees?

docs.title: Get Involved
docs.text: The Real Estate AI Task Force operates as an open-source policy coalition. Rather than relying on closed-door committees or outside consultants, we invite frontline practitioners, technologists, managing brokers, attorneys, and consumer advocates to contribute directly to our statutory frameworks and technical standards.

docs.title: Choose Your Contributor Track
docs.text:
To ensure productive collaboration without bureaucratic gridlock, participation is organized into four specialized tracks:

Contributor Track Who Should Join Core Responsibilities How to Apply / Participate 1. Technical & AI Systems Panel Brokerage CTOs, ML engineers, software architects, and PropTech builders. Stress-test human-in-the-loop checkpoints, audit-log standards, API boundaries, and technical definitions so laws work cleanly in production code. Open a Technical Panel Nomination via GitHub Issues or submit a technical RFC. 2. Brokerage Operations & Supervision Panel Managing brokers, compliance officers, and risk managers across independent and national firms. Evaluate broker supervision feasibility across varying firm sizes and prevent loopholes for unmonitored "thin-broker" models. Submit a Brokerage Panel Inquiry via GitHub Issues. 3. State Legislative & Legal Track Real estate attorneys, former state regulators, and ARA State Policy Chairs (priority: CA, NY, FL, TX). Adapt model statutory text to state-specific real estate codes, brief lawmakers, and coordinate with state real estate commissioners. Coordinate through ARA State Leadership or open a State Chapter Proposal on GitHub. 4. Public Request for Comments (RFC) Forum All licensed agents, consumers, housing advocates, and industry observers. Report real-world examples of unlicensed AI bots, submit contract edge cases, and provide line-by-line feedback on public drafts. Submit directly via our open Public RFC Portal.

docs.title: How to Submit Public Feedback (RFC Process)
docs.text:
Every draft of our model legislation and technical compliance standards is open for public review on GitHub:

  1. Review the Active Drafts: Read the current statutory principles and checkpoints on the Model Legislation page.
  2. Identify a Specific Issue: Focus your submission on a concrete statutory definition, technical edge case, or documented consumer harm scenario.
  3. Open a Structured RFC Issue: Visit the Codex Praedium Issues Portal, tag your submission with RFC-Feedback, and include:
  4. Jurisdiction / Context: Which state law or brokerage workflow is affected.
  5. Consumer or Fiduciary Risk: What harm occurs if the gap is left unaddressed.
  6. Proposed Amendment: Specific language or technical guardrail you recommend.

Attribution & Confidentiality Options: Public RFC submissions are archived transparently on GitHub. For enterprise engineering leaders or compliance officers joining our Advisory Panels, participation is available under Chatham House Rule (optional attribution) to respect corporate communications policies.

docs.title: Community Rules of Engagement
docs.text:
To maintain credibility with state legislators, attorneys general, and regulatory boards, all contributors must abide by our Code of Discourse:

  • Anchor in Consumer Protection: Frame all arguments around fiduciary duty, legal accountability, and public safety—never commission protectionism or anti-competitive restrictions.
  • Zero Vendor Pitching: Task Force forums and working groups are strictly non-commercial. Promoting, demoing, or soliciting leads for proprietary software products is prohibited.
  • Keep Marketing Separate: Discussions regarding virtual staging disclosures, listing copy prompts, or everyday agent AI tools belong in general practitioner forums rather than statutory drafting tracks.

docs.title: Institutional & Association Collaboration
docs.text: We welcome formal collaboration with state and local real estate associations, MLS organizations, and consumer protection groups. If your organization is drafting or evaluating state-level AI legislation, use our 3-Point Legislative Litmus Test as a shared baseline or open a collaborative working thread on GitHub.

docs.title: Prior Work & Media
docs.text: The Real Estate AI Task Force builds upon over a year of published legal research, technical gap analyses, trade press op-eds, and public roundtable debates. This archive documents the foundational work establishing the Licensee-in-the-Loop regulatory framework.

docs.title: Foundational White Papers & Policy Blueprints
docs.text:
• The Worthy Cause: Empower the Agent, Protect the Consumer Blueprint Real Estate Futures Blueprint (2025–2026) The inaugural policy paper examining how autonomous agentic AI systems perform regulated brokerage acts without licensure, exposing consumers to unmonitored liability while bypassing state real estate commissions.

  • NAR's Maginot Line: Unlicensed AI Bots vs. Human Fiduciaries Real Estate Futures Blueprint — October 28, 2026 An institutional analysis detailing why legacy federal-preemption strategies fail to protect consumers under state-based real estate license laws, and why grassroots, state-by-state legislative action is essential.

  • NAR's AI Strategy: My HousingWire OpEd Scores Support from NAR's Top Reformer Real Estate Futures Blueprint — September 30, 2026 An exclusive Q&A with Jason Haber (Co-Founder & President of the American Real Estate Association) outlining ARA's state-capital legislative strategy, fiduciary guardrails, and commitment to consumer safety over commission protectionism.

docs.title: Trade Media & Industry Commentary
docs.text: • NAR's AI Strategy: Why Real Estate Associations Must Lobby for 'Licensee-in-the-Loop' AI Laws HousingWire Op-Ed by Dmitriy Kruglyak — September 23, 2026 Examines the regulatory blind spot surrounding low-cost autonomous bots, featuring commentary from AI safety pioneer Professor Gary Marcus on why probabilistic models cannot substitute for human fiduciary accountability in mission-critical transactions.

docs.title: Public Panels & Video Roundtables
docs.text:
• Unlicensed AI Bots vs. Human Fiduciaries: The Battle for Real Estate's Future The STATE of Real Estate Roundtable — October 21, 2026 The industry's first open roundtable debate on autonomous agentic AI in real estate, featuring Jason Haber (ARA President), Dmitriy Kruglyak (Task Force Chair), Briggs Elwell, Ricky Carruth, and Eric Zollinger. Topics include:
  • How continuous-loop agentic AI differs from standard chat interfaces
  • Why state real estate commissioners face political hesitation enforcing against non-licensee tech startups without explicit legislative mandates
  • Real-world examples of AI contract hallucinations (such as missed addendum credits)
  • Early bicameral legislative progress in New York State

docs.title: Key Policy Takeaways Across Publications
docs.text:
Core Theme Summary of Findings State vs. Federal Jurisdiction Real estate licensure and fiduciary duties are governed exclusively at the state level; federal preemption efforts weaken local consumer enforcement. Low-Hanging Fruit vs. Systemic Risk Policing virtual staging photos among licensed agents is an easy distraction; the deeper threat is unlicensed software entities conducting end-to-end transactions for fees. Probabilistic Limits of AI Generative models guess token sequences and suffer from context deterioration, making pre-execution human licensee verification mandatory for binding contracts. Non-Delegable Supervision Brokerage supervision rules must evolve for an AI-first environment so managing brokers cannot use "thin broker" structures to rubber-stamp unmonitored bots.

Have relevant legal research, state regulatory filings, or technical case studies to add to the public archive? Submit a pull request or open an issue on GitHub.
